opus-5.5.text:
So the way I read that paper, Kendall and Gal are trying to separate two different kinds of uncertainty that people had tended to lump together. The first is what they call aleatoric uncertainty, which is the irreducible noise in the data itself. If a region of the image is blurry, or there's a boundary between two objects where the labels are inherently ambiguous, no amount of extra training data is going to make that go away. The second is epistemic uncertainty, which is the model's uncertainty about its own parameters, the kind of uncertainty that comes from not having seen enough data, and in principle it shrinks as you collect more.

Their approach to aleatoric uncertainty is fairly direct: they have the network output not just a prediction but also a variance term, and they train with a loss that lets the network attenuate the penalty on examples it considers noisy, at the cost of a log-variance regularizer so it can't just declare everything uncertain. That's heteroscedastic regression, and it works quite well for capturing input-dependent noise.

For epistemic uncertainty, they rely on Monte Carlo dropout, which Gal had developed earlier. You keep dropout turned on at test time, run the input through the network many times, and look at the variance of the predictions as an approximation to the posterior predictive variance.

My view is that the aleatoric part is solid and useful. I'm more skeptical about the epistemic part, though. MC dropout is a rather crude approximation to the posterior, and in my experience it doesn't reliably tell you when you've gone outside the training distribution. And that's precisely the case I care most about in open-world settings, where you encounter novel categories or objects the system has never seen. The dropout variance is computed over the representation the network has learned, and if a novel input simply doesn't activate any features that distinguish it, the network can be confidently wrong, and all the dropout samples will agree.

So I think the paper made an important conceptual contribution by clarifying the distinction and showing that both matter for things like segmentation and depth estimation. But I'd caution people against believing that MC dropout gives you a trustworthy measure of "the model doesn't know." For that, I think we need additional tools, things like anomaly or novelty detection on the representation, ensembles, and careful calibration on held-out data, rather than relying on one Bayesian approximation to do all the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes variance across MC dropout predictions as an approximation to posterior predictive variance, but does not identify disagreement among models that fit the observed data as the measure of epistemic uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It says the network outputs a variance term trained with a loss and log-variance regularizer, but does not describe using ensemble-derived variance estimates as supervised targets.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the key move in that paper is that they separate out two different kinds of uncertainty, and they argue that you need to handle them differently.

The first is what they call aleatoric uncertainty. That's the uncertainty that's inherent in the data itself, the noise. If you're doing depth estimation from a camera image, for example, there are regions, maybe a shiny surface or the far horizon, where the image just doesn't contain enough information to determine the depth, no matter how much training data you have. More data won't fix it. And their approach there is quite simple and, I think, elegant: you have the network predict not just the output, but also a variance for that output. So the network learns a mean and a noise level, and you train it with a loss that's essentially the negative log likelihood of a Gaussian, so that when the network can't predict well in some region, it's rewarded for saying so by inflating the predicted variance. One nice side effect is that this acts as a kind of learned attenuation: the noisy examples get down-weighted automatically during training, so the model doesn't waste capacity trying to fit them.

The second kind is epistemic uncertainty, which is the model's own uncertainty about what the right function is. That's the uncertainty you get from not having enough data in some part of the input space, and it does go away as you collect more data. For that they use Monte Carlo dropout, which is Gal's earlier idea that if you leave dropout turned on at test time and run the network several times, you get a crude approximation to sampling from a posterior over the weights. The spread across those samples is your estimate of epistemic uncertainty.

So the full model does both at once. You run multiple stochastic forward passes, each of which outputs a mean and a variance, and you combine the variance across passes with the average predicted noise. They also extend it to classification by putting the noise on the logits rather than directly on the output.

Now, my own view is that the decomposition is conceptually very useful, and it has been quite influential for that reason. But I'd put some caveats on it. The aleatoric part is only as good as the model's ability to recognize when it's in a noisy region, and that itself depends on having seen similar inputs during training. And the epistemic estimate from MC dropout is really a heuristic. It's not a well-calibrated posterior, and in particular it tends not to do a good job of flagging inputs that are genuinely far from the training distribution, which is the case I care most about from an open-world or safety standpoint. So I think of that paper as a very practical engineering recipe that gets you two useful signals, rather than a complete solution to the problem of knowing what the model doesn't know.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated stochastic passes approximate samples from a posterior over weights and that their spread estimates epistemic uncertainty, conveying disagreement among data-informed model samples.

r002.rationale: The response describes having the network predict variance and training it with a Gaussian negative log-likelihood, but does not describe ensemble-derived variance estimates used as supervised targets.

astra-6.text:
The way I understand their approach is that they’re trying to distinguish two sources of uncertainty. One is epistemic uncertainty, which is uncertainty about the model itself because we have limited training data. The other is aleatoric uncertainty, which comes from ambiguity or noise in the observations.

For the epistemic part, they use dropout as an approximation to Bayesian inference. You run the network multiple times with different dropout masks, and you look at how much its predictions vary. That gives you an indication of how uncertain the model is about its prediction.

For the aleatoric part, you train the network to predict not just an answer, but also a measure of the noise associated with that answer. In a regression problem, for example, it can output both a mean and a variance. And that variance can depend on the input, so the network can say, ‘This particular observation is harder to interpret.’ You train those outputs together using a likelihood objective, which penalizes prediction errors but also prevents the model from simply claiming enormous uncertainty everywhere.

The useful distinction is that more relevant training data can reduce epistemic uncertainty. It won’t necessarily resolve ambiguity inherent in the observation. And neither estimate is an automatic guarantee that the network will recognize every unfamiliar situation.

r001.rationale: The response describes epistemic uncertainty as prediction variation across dropout masks, but does not identify disagreement among models that fit the observed data.

r002.rationale: It says the network predicts a variance and trains it with a likelihood objective; it does not describe using ensemble-derived variance estimates as supervised targets.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the key distinction they make is between two sources of uncertainty. One is epistemic uncertainty, which is uncertainty about the model itself because we have limited training data. The other is aleatoric uncertainty, which comes from noise or ambiguity in the observations. Getting more training data can help with the first, but it doesn’t necessarily eliminate the second.

Their approach is to represent both. For epistemic uncertainty, they use an approximate Bayesian treatment of the network weights. With dropout, for example, you can run the same input through the network multiple times with different dropout masks and see how much the predictions vary.

For aleatoric uncertainty, they have the network predict the observation noise along with its prediction. So, in a regression problem, it might output both a mean and a variance, with that variance depending on the input. The training objective lets it assign greater uncertainty to difficult observations, but includes a penalty so it can’t simply declare everything uncertain.

Then you combine those two sources: how much the models disagree, and how much observation noise they predict. What I find useful about that distinction is that it tells you something about what might improve the prediction—whether you need more training examples, or whether the observation itself just doesn’t contain enough information.

r001.rationale: It treats variation across dropout-based weight samples’ predictions as epistemic uncertainty, conveying disagreement among model variants.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting observation-noise variance and training with a penalized objective, but not using ensemble-derived variance estimates as supervised targets.
